comparator.name: Law
comparator.sourceNotes: The dated 2026–2027 guide controls this generic Dutch full-time Law LLB. The curriculum introduced from 2023 is fully present across three sixty-credit years. Four compulsory Amsterdam Law Firm modules each carry zero credits; they remain required and are not added to the 180-EC total. The fifteen-credit Year-3 elective space remains open. Insolvency is retained from the original public-list ordering; the dated menu lists Labour Law first but permits either and provides no default. This is a restricted course choice, not a formal route. Law and Practice uses the permitted mediation/negotiation simulation rather than inventing an internship host. The thesis requires 120 EC already registered in SIS three weeks before semester start; completing both earlier years meets this condition before the selected Spring thesis. No fixed future cohort timetable is guaranteed beyond the dated curriculum.
components: The Dutch-taught Law LLB includes compulsory Amsterdam Law Firm 1.1 and 1.2 alongside Year-1 subjects. They carry zero additional credits and develop legal research, writing, oral advocacy and mediation.
Amsterdam Law Firm 2.1 is a compulsory zero-credit legal-research and writing module alongside Year 2. The research plan must receive at least 5 before the research report may be written.

Amsterdam Law Firm 2.2 is a compulsory zero-credit moot-court module. Its criminal-law or administrative-law variant is taken alongside, or after, the relevant substantive and procedural courses. This pathway completes both sets in Year 2.

This example chooses the permitted mediation and negotiation simulation. Students act as mediators in a legal case, practising listening, perspective-taking and negotiation. No internship host or placement is assumed.
Fifteen credits remain genuinely open for electives, a minor or study abroad. No particular course package, host or minor is imposed.

Insolvency Law is the retained permitted integration choice, combining earlier private-law subjects, company law and questions of distribution and justice. Labour Law is an alternative, not an additional component.
Fundamental Rights integrates earlier constitutional, European and international law with legal philosophy and applications across legal fields.

Entry requires at least 120 degree credits already recorded in SIS three weeks before the semester begins; expected but unregistered results do not count. Both earlier years are completed before the Spring thesis. The thesis includes an individual legal paper and oral presentation and defence before two assessors; no fiscal specialisation or particular topic is assumed.

courses: Business & Economy in the Age of AI
New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory

core: Legal foundations, reasoning, interpretation and the consequences of legal decisions
Public, constitutional, administrative and criminal law in a democratic society
Private, property, contract, family, corporate and insolvency law
Legal research, writing, case analysis, procedure and practical dispute work
adjacent: Digitalisation, platforms, artificial intelligence and law
Law, behaviour, society and the social impact of legal choices
Legal philosophy, professional ethics and responsibility
questions: How should legal institutions uphold democracy, rights and the rule of law?
How should private and commercial disputes be interpreted and resolved?
How do international, European and domestic legal orders interact?

trace: develops scholarly reading, research questions, academic writing, reflection and civic collaboration as the common foundation
develops financial statements, accounting, organisational control, accountability and discounted-cash-flow appraisal, providing actual financial analysis for enterprise decisions
examines AI, firms, regulation, corporate responsibility, labour and inequality through business and country research, providing an institutional perspective on innovative-company governance
examines legal frameworks for cross-border contracts, trade, finance, intellectual property and digital commerce, with advisory assignments and simulated arbitration

examines financial instruments, valuation, banks, risk, regulation and monetary institutions, with bank simulation and evidence-based financial decisions; it complements corporate financing rather than teaching company-law doctrine
introduces economic choice, markets, strategic interaction and government’s economic role as specific foundations for analysing regulation
examines incentives, uncertainty, strategic behaviour, markets and externalities as economic mechanisms that complement analysis of legal rules and regulation
examines public goods, taxation, spending, externalities and redistribution through policy models and research; this is an economic contribution rather than tax-law doctrine

develops causal and predictive economic-data analysis using regression estimators, tests and Monte Carlo simulation, with an empirical paper; this is a complementary analytical method rather than legal-doctrinal research
examines business strategy and responsible digital transformation, providing a concrete organisational account of how technological change creates governance problems
develops planning, collection, analysis and communication of market evidence, supporting empirical understanding of commercial decisions without claiming legal research methods
examines trade, institutions, policy conflict and cross-border business decisions, supporting the international commercial context of legal practice
develops business models and the functions of enterprises, providing organisational context and the formal foundation for transnational business law without claiming company-law doctrine
develops empirical design, measurement, statistics and a data-collection project as a methodological complement to socio-legal inquiry
examines motivation, leadership, teams, power, conflict and organisational change, including evidence synthesis for organisational cases
develops bargaining, interests, power, trust and strategic conflict management through negotiation simulations and scenario design
introduces legal traditions, public/private law, justice and social context through case briefs, legal interpretation, mock trials and a socio-legal proposal

examines nationalism, imperialism, war, revolution, decolonisation and modern state/society transformations through historical evidence, supplying a specific historical dimension for public and international institutions
examines human-rights law, protection institutions, landmark cases and philosophical justifications through legal and normative argument
examines criminal liability, punishment, criminalisation, excuses, offences and participation, with legal-advice memoranda and a criminology research proposal
examines international legal sources, state responsibility, institutions, force, human rights and treaty politics through legal cases and critical research
compares constitutional structures, rights, courts and judicial review, with administrative participation, remedies and procedural fairness
examines property, tort and contract rights across legal systems through legal briefs, comparative contract research and simulated mediation
examines EU institutions, competences, legal effect, remedies, citizenship and free movement through current judgments and legal cases
develops ethical interpretation, normative argument and independent positions on moral theory and practical questions relevant to legal judgement
examines rights, authority, social order and political legitimacy through primary philosophical texts and normative argument, complementing jurisprudential questions
compares democracy, institutions, political actors and participation through empirical concepts, measurement and research, providing substantive political analysis of constitutional democracy
examines state relations, international institutions, conflict and cooperation through theories and cases, with a UN simulation and researched negotiation
examines EU integration, institutions, legislation, representation and legitimacy, with empirical parliamentary research that complements EU legal analysis
examines policymaking and analytical frameworks through a public-policy case and policy memos, complementing legal analysis of government decisions
examines conflict, humanitarian law, human rights, peacebuilding and transitional justice through interdisciplinary research and a policy brief
examines social institutions, inequality, identity and boundaries through social theory and evidence, complementing analysis of law’s social context
develops qualitative design, interviews, documentary inquiry, coding and interpretation for empirical investigation of social and institutional questions
examines environmental-justice movements, collective action and feminist/anticolonial perspectives through actual environmental cases
examines civil society, trust, public spheres, solidarity and social repair through theory and research on an organisation or movement, supporting the public-law option’s civil-society perspective
develops rhetorical analysis, argument construction, debating and public speaking; its communication contribution is distinguished from legal procedure
examines persuasion, framing, argumentation and ethics through research and community projects, supporting professional communication rather than supplying courtroom doctrine

candidates.label: Private law, business and commercial relations

selection.assessment: The closest interdisciplinary law-and-society programme owns the broad direct interests. Two distinct feasible directions deepen the public/international/European and private/commercial sides of the curriculum. Together these reach the three-alternative maximum.

alternatives.label: Law, politics & society
alternatives.labelReason: Study law through comparative private, criminal, constitutional, human-rights, European, international and transnational business law. Political institutions, social theory, economics, ethics, empirical inquiry and AI governance examine how legal rules operate in society and respond to institutional and technological change.
alternatives.concept: Study law through comparative private, criminal, constitutional, human-rights, European, international and transnational business law. Political institutions, social theory, economics, ethics, empirical inquiry and AI governance examine how legal rules operate in society and respond to institutional and technological change.
progression: All assigned terms and earlier formal prerequisites were checked against the active workbook. Law/business gateways precede dependent legal courses, statistics precedes dependent economic and negotiation courses, and introductory economics precedes advanced economic analysis. Where selected, introductory comparative politics and sociology precede advanced EU and civil-society study.

alternatives.label: Public, international & European law
alternatives.labelReason: Study public, international and European law through human rights, constitutional structures, criminal justice and cross-border legal institutions. Comparative politics, public policy, international relations, history, sociology, economics and ethics examine state authority, democracy, conflict and environmental justice.
alternatives.concept: Study public, international and European law through human rights, constitutional structures, criminal justice and cross-border legal institutions. Comparative politics, public policy, international relations, history, sociology, economics and ethics examine state authority, democracy, conflict and environmental justice.
alternatives.distinctness: This option concentrates on public authority and cross-border institutions through comparative politics, EU politics, public policy, international relations, modern history, conflict and environmental justice. It replaces the closest option’s private law, transnational business law, AI-governance and negotiation strand with sustained public/international analysis.
progression: All assigned terms and earlier formal prerequisites were checked against the active workbook. Law/business gateways precede dependent legal courses, statistics precedes dependent economic and negotiation courses, and introductory economics precedes advanced economic analysis. Where selected, introductory comparative politics and sociology precede advanced EU and civil-society study.

alternatives.label: Private law, business & commercial relations
alternatives.labelReason: Study private and commercial legal relationships through private, criminal, constitutional, human-rights, international, European and transnational business law. Accounting, finance, economic analysis, digital strategy, organisations, negotiation and empirical business research examine the transactions and institutions within which legal problems arise.
alternatives.concept: Study private and commercial legal relationships through private, criminal, constitutional, human-rights, international, European and transnational business law. Accounting, finance, economic analysis, digital strategy, organisations, negotiation and empirical business research examine the transactions and institutions within which legal problems arise.
alternatives.distinctness: This option devotes sustained space to accounting, finance, digital business strategy, organisations, negotiation, econometrics and market research alongside actual legal study. The closest and public options place greater weight on political theory, comparative institutions, policy, conflict and social inquiry.
progression: All assigned terms and earlier formal prerequisites were checked against the active workbook. Law/business gateways precede dependent legal courses, statistics precedes dependent economic and negotiation courses, and introductory economics precedes advanced economic analysis. Where selected, introductory comparative politics and sociology precede advanced EU and civil-society study.

blocks: Law, public institutions, business and complementary disciplines

Both examine AI, institutional change, governance and regulation. UCR studies business/economic and social implications; UvA develops legal analysis of digitalisation, platforms and government algorithms.

Both examine contractual obligations, risk allocation, performance and remedies through legal cases. UCR concentrates on transnational commercial transactions; UvA develops Dutch contract and liability doctrine.

Both develop negotiation, conflicting perspectives and structured dispute-resolution practice. UCR uses bargaining simulations; the chosen UvA pathway uses mediation and negotiation around a legal case with explicit reflection on professional roles.
Both develop the nature of law, legal sources, interpretation and case analysis within a social and normative framework.
Both examine fundamental-rights law, protection institutions and philosophical justifications. UvA integrates the operation of rights across Dutch and international legal fields.
Both examine criminal acts, causation, intent, guilt, offences, justifications, excuses and participation as substantive grounds and limits of criminal liability.
Both develop public international law through legal sources, institutions, state responsibility, force and contemporary legal cases. The relationship is substantive but partial.

Both examine state organisation, rights, government powers and constitutional constraints. UCR compares systems and includes administrative principles; UvA establishes Dutch constitutional and administrative law.
Both develop contract, tort and property concepts through legal problems. UCR compares legal systems; UvA establishes Dutch private-law foundations including their social context.
Both examine the EU legal order, institutions, national effects, citizenship, free movement and remedies.
Both develop reasoned ethical positions on conflicting obligations. UCR provides general ethical theory and practical argument; UvA applies professional codes and role-specific dilemmas for lawyers.

Both examine normative foundations of rights, authority and the liberal political/legal order. UvA additionally develops specific jurisprudential theories, legal positivism, natural law and legal interpretation.
Both substantively examine constitutional democracy, institutions, representation and threats to democratic order. UCR uses empirical comparison; UvA develops a legal constitutional-redesign project.
Other dedicated Law requirements and open choice
The selected legal courses have their strongest primary relationships elsewhere; no additional course is counted for this dedicated Dutch legal component.
The selected legal courses have their strongest primary relationships elsewhere; no additional course is counted for this dedicated Dutch legal component.
Empirical methods and social study contribute elsewhere, but no additional course provides dedicated empirical analysis of how legal rules work in practice.
Selected private-law study does not provide a dedicated Dutch persons/family-law course.
The selected legal courses have their strongest primary relationships elsewhere; no additional course is counted for this dedicated Dutch legal component.
Modern political history is complementary context, not the historical study of legal sources and legal systems required here.
Private and commercial law contribute elsewhere; no separate course provides this integrated legal project on damages, compensation and asserting claims.
The selected legal courses have their strongest primary relationships elsewhere; no additional course is counted for this dedicated Dutch legal component.
The selected legal courses have their strongest primary relationships elsewhere; no additional course is counted for this dedicated Dutch legal component.
The selected legal courses have their strongest primary relationships elsewhere; no additional course is counted for this dedicated Dutch legal component.
Environmental justice, public policy and international-law study provide complementary perspectives, but no course reproduces this legal sustainability project and citizen-deliberation exercise.
Fifteen credits remain genuinely open; no minor, exchange host or elective package is invented.
Negotiation has its strongest relationship with the chosen Law and Practice pathway. No additional course supplies dedicated Dutch civil procedure.
Business and transnational commercial courses do not provide the dedicated Dutch corporate/legal-person formation, representation, governance and liability sequence.
Financial instruments and banking are complementary to insolvency questions, but do not supply insolvency doctrine, creditor ranking or bankruptcy procedure.
No scheduled UCR course is the compulsory legal bachelor thesis. Optional independent research is displayed separately outside scheduled credits.

notes.text: UvA provides a prescribed Dutch legal degree with Amsterdam Law Firm skills training, doctrinal and procedural depth, legal projects and a compulsory thesis. UCR combines substantial comparative and international law with related political, social and business study. The partial relationships shown do not reproduce this specialist sequence or confer legal professional qualification.

audience.programmeDescription: Law at UvA develops broad Dutch legal knowledge, academic legal reasoning and practical skills through the Amsterdam Law Firm. The programme combines private, public, criminal, European and international law with legal projects, open elective space and a required thesis. This example chooses Insolvency Law and the mediation/negotiation practice pathway.
audience.comparisonExplanation: UCR can combine substantial legal study with politics and society, public and international institutions, or private and commercial relations. Its law courses use comparative and international perspectives. UvA provides a deeper prescribed Dutch doctrinal and professional-practice sequence; the relationships shown are partial.
